To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
CADASIL mutations affect cysteine residues in EGF-like repeat 3-5, and that these mutations result in misfolding of the first six domains.

CADASIL is caused by small in-frame deletations and missense mutations that affect cysteine residues in EGF-like repeat domain 1-5 of the Notch3 receptor and that the misfolding of the first six EGFr domains of Notch-3 is a likely pathomechanism of CADASIL.

(i) CADASIL is caused by mutations in the Notch3 receptor gene; (ii) mutations are clustered within the EGF-like repeat domain region of Notch3; (iii) mutations are either in-frame deletions or missense mutations; (iv) 3D homological models predict misfolds for some of these mutations.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the elucidation of the genetic and pathogenetic mechanisms in CADASIL.
the identification of CADASIL mutations and the prediction of their potential effects on Notch3 structure and function.
the identification of mutations in the CADASIL gene and the analysis of their potential pathogenicity.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
CADASIL is a disorder of Notch3 protein folding, caused by mutations in the Notch3 EGF-like repeat domain.
mutations in the Notch3 EGF domains result in misfolding of the protein and thus lead to the disease.
mutations in the first five EGFDs of Notch3 are the cause of the majority of CADASIL cases.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
CADASIL is caused by a gain-of-function mechanism due to misfolding of EGF domains.
CADASIL is caused by missense mutations and small in-frame deletional mutations that affect cysteine residues and that result in misfolding of the EGF-like repeat domain.
CADASIL mutations in Notch3 result in the misfolding and mislocalisation of Notch3 EGF domains.
The main takeaway from our work is that
CADASIL can be caused by a variety of mutations in Notch3 and that these mutations are not clustered within a small region of the protein.
CADASIL mutations are small, mostly missense and affect the first five EGD-like domains.
the CADASIL mutations in EGF domains of Notch 3 are clustered in the first five domains, and the majority of them are missense mutations affecting the cysteine residues in the first EGF-like repeats.
